characterization_methods.key_findings: For the 19Al alloy the 550 °C/10 h condition shows a β-Mn matrix with fine 'New precipitates'; β-Mn is thermally activated and slow in this highest-Al alloy (Fig. 9).

characterization_methods.key_findings: EBSD of the 19Al alloy reveals the α→β-Mn transformation and new BCC and FCC precipitates inside β-Mn; solution-treated alloys are single-phase α (BCC). (19Al EBSD maps shown for 525 °C/10 h, 600 °C/3 h, 650 °C/6 h — not directly the 550 °C/10 h condition.)
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Scanning step size 1.5 μm (low magnification) and 0.05 μm (high magnification)
characterization_methods.purpose: Identify phases (α/BCC, β-Mn, α-Mn, FCC) and their evolution with aging

characterization_methods.key_findings: For the 19Al alloy the XRD pattern was collected on the 550 °C/6 h sample (not the 550 °C/10 h sample) and shows α/D0₃ together with α-Mn and β-Mn peaks, indicating α-Mn and β-Mn co-precipitation before the α matrix fully transforms.
characterization_methods.purpose: Identify constituent phases in aged alloys

interfaces.interface_notes: TEM characterization of the β-Mn/FCC Cu-rich phase interfaces (FCC twins, HRTEM/FFT) was performed on the 15Al (600 °C/6 h) and 17Al (575 °C/6 h) peak-hardness samples, not directly on the 19Al 550 °C/10 h sample; the general statement that new BCC and FCC Cu-rich phases form at the interfaces between β-Mn applies to the ultra-hard Fe-Mn-Al-Cu alloys.
interfaces.phase_evolution: α → α + FCC Cu-rich phase → α-Mn + β-Mn + BCC phase → β-Mn + BCC phase + FCC Cu-rich phase. For the 19Al alloy, the α→β-Mn transformation at 550 °C required 10 h; new BCC and FCC Cu-rich phases form at the β-Mn interfaces once the matrix has transformed.

phase_interfaces.phase_2_name: FCC Cu-rich phase / BCC phase (new precipitates)

comparative_performance.comparison_metric: Among the Fe-Mn-Al-Cu alloys, increasing Al content slows the β-Mn precipitation kinetics and lowers the final hardening effect; for the 19Al alloy at 550 °C the full α→β-Mn transformation required 10 h (vs 6 h for 17Al).

processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Ingots with nominal composition Fe-35Mn-19Al-5Cu (at.%) produced by melting high-purity (>99.9 %) raw materials in a vacuum induction furnace under argon atmosphere.
Homogenized ingots hot-rolled into plates with a thickness of 4 mm.
Plates cut into 10 × 5 × 2 mm³ samples for Vickers hardness and microstructure characterizations.
Samples solution treated at 1100 °C for 10 min under argon atmosphere followed by oil quenching (parent process proc_st-1100c-10min-oq).
Solution-treated samples aged at 550 °C for 10 h followed by water quenching — defines this sample (19Al 550 °C/10 h).

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Vickers microhardness measured with an HVS-1000 digital microhardness tester, load 9.8 N for 15 s; each sample tested 5 times and value reported as the average.

structures.overall_structure: In the 19Al alloy aged at 550 °C for 10 h the α (BCC) matrix had almost completely transformed into β-Mn; because Al content slows the precipitation kinetics of β-Mn, this highest-Al alloy required the full 10 h at 550 °C for the α→β-Mn transformation to be nearly complete. Numerous fine 'new precipitates' (BCC and FCC Cu-rich phases) are distributed within/at the interfaces of the β-Mn.

unmapped_findings: The 19Al solution-treated baseline Vickers hardness is 263.8 ± 1.1 HV (Table 4); this is the common baseline for all 19Al aging conditions and belongs to the solution-treated (pre-aging) state rather than to the 550 °C/10 h aged sample.

The XRD pattern for the 19Al alloy was collected on the 550 °C × 6 h sample (not the 550 °C × 10 h sample) and reveals α/D0₃ + α-Mn + β-Mn reflections (Fig. 10), showing that α-Mn and β-Mn co-precipitate before full α→β-Mn transformation.

The fracture toughness KIC = 3.5 MPa·m^1/2 and average indentation crack length of 35 μm reported for the 19Al alloy correspond to its hardest (peak-hardness) sample (600 °C/10 h, 917.8 HV), not to the 550 °C/10 h condition.
The volume fraction of FCC Cu-rich + BCC precipitates for the 19Al alloy (6.5 %) was measured on the 650 °C/6 h sample (Vickers hardness 810.9 HV), not on the 550 °C/10 h sample.

The β-Mn intrinsic hardness of the hardest 19Al sample (12.5 ± 0.4 GPa) and the average nanoindentation hardness (10.4 ± 1.3 GPa), as well as the β-Mn SEM-EDS composition (Mn 36.2, Al 17.5, Cu 2.6 at.%), were measured on the hardest 19Al sample (600 °C/10 h), not on the 550 °C/10 h sample.

The Fe-Mn-Al-Cu alloy series achieved an ultra-wide flexible Vickers hardness of 253.4–965.6 HV and a maximum specific hardness >140 HV·cm³/g; the paper's specific value of 141 HV·cm³/g (and the density 6.66 g/cm³ for 19Al) is attributed to the 15Al alloy (Fe-35.2Mn-15Al-5.2Cu), not to the 19Al alloy.
